query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Enhanced corrosion resistance in steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily due to a homogenized microstructure that minimizes detrimental elemental segregation (particularly at grain boundaries), thereby facilitating the formation of a uniform, self-healing passivating oxide layer—rich in chromium—which effectively blocks corrosive species.
generation.material_initial_state: Commercial stainless steels with typical alloying elements (e.g., Cr, Ni) that, in their as-received or conventionally processed state, exhibit variable levels of elemental segregation at grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled heat treatments (annealing) designed to reduce grain boundary segregation and promote a homogeneous distribution of passivating elements, followed by standardized surface finishing.
generation.conditions: Expose both treated and untreated steel samples to environments that mimic chemical-processing (e.g., acidic solutions like 0.5M H2SO4) and nuclear-power conditions (elevated temperatures in high-purity water), under controlled laboratory settings.
generation.structural_mediator: The continuity and composition of the passivating oxide film—particularly the distribution of chromium—and the grain boundary chemistry.
generation.mechanism: Heat treatment reduces localized elemental segregation, ensuring a uniform availability of passivating elements (e.g., chromium) across the microstructure. This uniformity aids in the rapid formation of a defect‐free, self-healing oxide layer that limits ion transport and suppresses localized corrosion initiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Steel samples with minimized segregation (via the tailored heat treatment) will exhibit a wider passivation potential, lower corrosion current densities, and a more uniform, adherent, and chemically stable oxide film compared to untreated samples.
generation.baseline: Untreated or conventionally processed steels that show heterogeneous grain-boundary segregation and less uniform passive film formation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold under controlled laboratory test conditions that simulate the chemical environment of processing plants and the aqueous conditions of nuclear reactors. In scenarios dominated by factors such as severe mechanical wear or conditions far outside these parameters, the beneficial effect may be reduced.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of improvement in corrosion resistance and the exact microstructural markers can vary depending on the specific steel grade, precise alloy composition, and the parameters of the applied heat treatment.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of steel samples: one set receives optimized annealing to minimize grain boundary segregation and the other set remains untreated. Subject both sets to simulated corrosive environments (acidic solution for chemical-processing and high-temperature water for nuclear-power conditions). Use microscopic and spectroscopic techniques to examine the oxide layer, and perform electrochemical tests (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization) to measure corrosion rates.
measurements: Grain boundary chemistry and elemental distribution (via EDS and XPS)
Oxide film uniformity and adherence (via SEM/TEM)
Corrosion current density and passivation potential (via electrochemical testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the optimized (annealed) samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in passivation behavior and lower corrosion rates relative to the untreated samples, thereby showing similar oxide film characteristics, the hypothesis that reduced elemental segregation enhances corrosion resistance would be falsified.

Corrosion Resistance of Al0.5CoCrFeNiCuxAgy (x = 0.25, 0.5; y = 0, 0.1) High-Entropy Alloys in 0.5M H2SO4 Solution

Abstract: AbstractThe electrochemical behavior of the as-cast Al0.5CoCrFeNiCuxAgy (x = 0.25, 0.5; y = 0, 0.1) high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in a 0.5M H2SO4 solution was studied. Polarization measurements were carried out in a standard three-electrode electrochemical cell at room temperature using a platinum counter electrode and a saturated silver chloride reference electrode. For Al0.5CoCrFeNiCu0.5 and Al0.5CoCrFeNiCu0.5Ag0.1, copper segregation along the grain boundaries was observed, which highly dissolved in the sulfuric acid solution and resulted in low corrosion resistance of the samples. Introducing Ag into Al0.5CoCrFeNiCu0.25 HEA led to the precipitation of a copper–silver eutectic structure, in which the copper regions were selectively dissolved in the sulfuric acid solution. Al0.5CoCrFeNiCu0.25 exhibited the best corrosion resistance with the corrosion current density of Icorr = 3.52 ± 0.02 μA/cm2, significantly superior to that of the Al0.5CoCrFeNi sample without copper and silver (Icorr = 6.05 ± 0.05 μA/cm2).
